chunks: And everything in this book that is narrated from Ubayd ibn Zurarah has been transmitted by me from my father - may Allah be pleased with him - from Sa'd ibn Abdullah, from Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn ibn Abi Al-Khattab, from Al-Hakam ibn Miskin Al-Thaqafi, from Ubayd ibn Zurarah ibn A'yun, and he was known to have a squint.

key_terms.أَحْوَلَ: Cross-eyed or squint-eyed, a physical descriptor used to distinguish individuals.
key_terms.الثَّقَفِيِّ: Al-Thaqafi, a nisba indicating affiliation with the Thaqif tribe.
key_terms.رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ: May Allah be pleased with him, a phrase of respect often used for the narrator's father.
key_terms.عُبَيْدُ بْنُ زُرَارَةَ: Ubayd ibn Zurarah, a prominent companion of the Imams and a key narrator.

ai.seo_question: How is the chain of narration for Ubayd ibn Zurarah's hadiths verified in Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih?
ai.summary: This passage from *Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih* demonstrates Shaykh al-Saduq’s rigorous methodology in verifying the authenticity of narrations by explicitly tracing the *isnad* back to Ubayd ibn Zurarah, a prominent companion of Imam al-Sadiq. By detailing the specific chain of transmission and noting Ubayd’s distinctive physical trait (*ahwal*), al-Saduq reinforces the reliability of the report and provides a tangible identifier for the narrator within the scholarly tradition.
